title: The pilgrimages
hookLine: tradition says he traveled with Sikhs to pilgrim sites and spoke against the pilgrim tax

lines: A FAMILY AT THE RIVER GATE.
cards: Pay here before you pray. A gate at the edge of a holy river, and someone collecting a fee from every traveler who wants to bathe. A family has walked for days.
They're tired, they've saved for this, and now there's a charge just to reach the water.
Sikh tradition tells of Guru Amar Das traveling with his Sikhs to pilgrim places, the crowded river towns where people came to bathe and remember God.
And it remembers him speaking up about a tax laid on the pilgrims themselves.

teach.b: Why would a Guru go to a pilgrim town at all? The Sikh Gurus taught that the true pilgrimage is inward.
Guru Nanak puts it plainly in the Japji, paraphrased: I would bathe at the place of pilgrimage if that pleased Him; without pleasing Him, what good is the bathing?
The Sikh word for a pilgrim place is tirath, and the Japji itself speaks of bathing at a tirath within.

teach.h: HE WENT WHERE THE PEOPLE WERE.
teach.b: So Sikh tellings present it this way: he went where the people already were. Seekers gathered there, hungry for God, and the Guru met them in the crowd, sang the Word, and fed people.

Not to mock their journey, but to share what the Gurus had found. Then the tax. Tradition says the Guru spoke against a charge laid on pilgrims, and some accounts say the emperor Akbar later lifted it.

teach.h: NO PRICE TO COME NEAR GOD.
teach.b: Whatever the details, the instinct runs through the stories of his time: no one should have to pay to come near God.
Tradition says the well at Goindval was open to every caste. The langar row asks no fee. The Guru's Word is sung for anyone who walks in.
A tax on pilgrims put a price on the very thing the Gurus kept giving away.
So the line has two sides: free pilgrims from unfair charges, and remember that the pilgrimage inward needs no gate at all.

how: Sikhs tell the stories of Guru Amar Das's journeys and the pilgrim tax in histories and katha, and they speak of an inward pilgrimage; gurdwaras are open to visitors without any fee.

o: the Guru among pilgrims, against a tax to reach God
a vow to visit every holy river before death
the Guru's travels to collect a pilgrim tax

p: where the Japji says to bathe
a charge to come near God
bathing is good only if it pleases Him

s: the Guru went to pilgrim towns to mock the pilgrims

games.q: pilgrims must pay a tax to reach the holy water. you're the Guru, traveling among them. what do you do?
o: say nothing; it's not your concern.
tell the pilgrims to stop going.
games.why: tradition says he spoke against it. no one, in the Gurus' teaching, should have to pay to come near God.

practice: Think of a cost someone has to pay just to belong, worship, learn or be helped, a fee, a form, a rule, a look at the door, in your workplace, your town or your own house.
Hold it without anger and ask simply: who does this keep out, and does it need to? Then let the breath carry you to the tirath within that the Japji speaks of, and if you pray, say Waheguru there.

wordCard.voice: The pilgrimages. Guru Amar Das, tradition says, went among the pilgrims, shared the Word, and spoke against a tax that charged them to come near God. Today's word.

orig.note: a place of pilgrimage; the Japji also speaks of a tirath within.

carryVoice: Your line: free pilgrims. No one should have to pay to come near God. Until tomorrow, then.
